replying_to: Replying to POLAR: A Polynomial Arithmetic Framework for Verifying Neural-Network Controlled Systems
display_title: Official Review of Paper3942 by Reviewer zrk4

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors attack a significant problem or bounded-time reachability analysis of neural-network controlled systems (NNCSs). The method allows for verification of decision-making procedures applied by trained neural networks to systems with the known continuous model (continuous plants).

The claimed main novelty of the paper is the application of the basic Taylor Model arithmetic in combination with the univariate Bernstein polynomial interpolation to handle non-differentiable NN activation functions.

The algorithm is tested in a set of benchmarks introduced in the other related work. 

The main theoretical result states that the TM flow pipes computed using the POLAR approach are state-wise approximations for the reachable sets.
content.main_review:
The authors propose a new algorithm improving bounded-time reachability analysis of neural-network controlled systems (POLAR). POLAR is based on the previous works, the method is sound, and improves a set of benchmarks introduced in related work, the reported improvement of POLAR over other related work in Table 1 concerns the runtime & benchmark coverage.

I have significant concerns about the paper and the presented results, I summarize all of my major concerns below.

### 1. The method seems not suitable for deep (reinforcement) learning practice.

I have significant doubts regarding the applicability of the proposed method in deep-learning, reinforcement learning & high dimensional dynamics modeling context. The first sentence of the introduction reads _“Neural networks have been increasingly used as the central decision-makers in a variety of tasks Mnih et al. (2015); Lillicrap et al. (2016); Pan et al. (2018)”_, where authors indicate solving examples of reinforcement learning controllers applied to Atari benchmarks/continuous robotic environments.  This class of problems is characterized by the high dimensionality of the environment model itself (e.g. dim. of rigid body actuator state vectors in robotics / dim of pixel screen in Atari games/complexity of the learned world model). The dimensionality of those problems certainly exceeds greatly the dimensions of the studied benchmarks - the number of state variables varies from two to four, and the number of neurons in each layer is 20. 
I gave some thought if the Taylor model + Bernstein interpolation approach is scalable. Unfortunately, my conclusion is negative. I think such an approach does not scale up. AFAIK Taylor’s model approach requires to recursively compute the polynomial coefficients. The cost of computation depends on the state dimension, the complexity of the plant vector field (M_F), and on top of that, the computation order is quadratic w.r.t. the Taylor polynomial degree. Then the nonlinear activations are Bernstein interpolated, multiplying the overall complexity by a quadratic factor w.r.t. the Bernstein polynomial order times the NN depth. Unless the authors convince me otherwise, this does not seem to scale up for larger (>10) orders of polynomials and states. There are no details given of how one of the crucial parts of the algorithm - the linear-nonlinear part decomposition is being performed. This computation may be of significant complexity. I could not find exact order numbers employed by the authors to see what problems are reachable using the approach at all.

###  2. Concerns regarding the novelty of the approach

I like to contest the claimed novelty of the proposed method claimed in the introduction. The polynomial arithmetic framework does not seem to be novel.  A Taylor model + Bernstein polynomials approach was already introduced in j. Fan et. al. _"ReachNN*: A tool for reachability analysis of neural-network controlled systems"_. Even the studied benchmarks are the same as in the related work. The only new element considers neuron-wise Bernstein polynomial interpolation, which seems to be a straightforward modification over the related work algorithm. The symbolic reminders is also not a new idea, as noted, it is adapted from Chen & Sankaranarayanan (2016) (for ODEs), but I believe it circulated in interval analysis literature even earlier (see the next paragraph). Overall, I rather see the algorithm as an improved ReachNN*, rather than a standalone tool, deserving a new acronym (POLAR). 

###  3. Related work is not presented, the bibliography is not complete.

The bibliography can certainly be improved. The related work section misses any discussion and comparison of the other than TM techniques for computation of overestimation of reachable sets of nonlinear dynamical systems; also the provided list of related work does not seem to be complete. The wrapping effect, widely mentioned in interval analysis literature already appeared in original works by R. Moore, dating back to 60's, is here attributed to Jaulin et al. (2001). AFAIK the idea of not computing the term A*I directly but rather keeping separate coordinate system (matrix A) and the intervals (interval vector I) goes back to R. Lohner _“Computation of Guaranteed Enclosures for the Solutions of Ordinary Initial and Boundary Value Problems”_, 1992. Also see the book: U Kulisch, R Lohner, A Facius, _“Perspectives on Enclosure Methods”_, 2001, Springer.

### 4. Not Clear Benchmarks.

The proposed benchmarks are taken from a related work paper entitled: “ReachNN: Reachability Analysis of Neural-Network Controlled Systems, “ not presented on a machine learning venue. The examples are not even presented in the paper. Only rough information about their dimensionality is given. It is unclear what a single test was about at all. This is a serious flaw, which assumes the knowledge of the previous work and refers to another paper to know what the studied benchmarks are.  It is also clear that the used examples are much smaller than the ones used in deep learning practice. There is no information given how the controllers were trained /synthesized, no information available on how the tool is implemented, does it use any external libraries. If it is possible to provide a NN controller that was obtained using standard e.g. PyTorch machine learning toolkit. 

### 5. Choice of the employed benchmark metrics.

Table 1 summarizing the results in the main text provides a single metric used for comparison i.e., the runtime in seconds. As the benchmark problems are not presented at all, it is hard to decide about the significance of the obtained results in comparison to existing tools.  The benchmarks seem to be highly dependent on integration time-horizon, polynomial approximation orders, and time-stepping,  none of which is provided in the paper. Also, a discussion of another comparison metric - tightness of bounds is deferred to the appendix, where just plots allowing for visual comparison are provided. It would make sense to quantify the benchmarks using the final enclosure volume / average enclosure volume.

### Other remarks: 

* p.7: What do you mean by decomposing function into the linear and the remaining part in q_i ? I guess there is no unique decomposition q_i(y) = Q_i*y + q_i^R(y).
* eq. top of p. 6: symbol L_j is not introduced,
* p.12 end of B.1: what citation ‘[a]’ supposed to mean?
* p.12/13 B.2 proof: No reference given for the ‘Base Case’ part of the proof, i.e. that TM flow-pipe construction for the ode with control variable is sound. Another gap is an argument that the Bernstein polynomial interpolation layer-by-layer of the NN controller is also sound, this does not look obvious to me.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The studied problem and the algorithm itself are nice. However, I have significant doubts about the algorithm novelty, the reported benchmarks, the practicality of the method, and the presentation and completeness of the paper. All of my concerns are summarized in the five paragraphs above. 

Concluding, I think that the paper’s flaws overweight its advantages, and hence, unfortunately, I recommend a rejection of the paper in its present form.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3942 by Reviewer zrk4

content.title: To Reviewer zrk4 (Part 1)
content.comment:
We would like to first point out that the reviewer misunderstands both this paper and ReachNN*, and is unfair on the novelty assessment: 1) ReachNN* paper does not combine Taylor model and Bernstein polynomials when dealing with the neural network controller. It only uses Bernstein polynomials to directly approximate the network end-to-end through sampling the input space. 
POLAR is the FIRST work that combines Taylor models and Bernstein polynomials (among other novel contributions) to compute the function (over)approximation of a neural network. 2) The symbolic remainder technique itself has been proposed for ODE reachable set computation. However, it has been never used in handling neural networks prior to this work, and POLAR is the FIRST work that uses symbolic remainder to address the wrapping effect in the Taylor model propagation in a neural network. 
If the reviewer questions our novelty because a fundamental mathematical technique is used, albeit in very different places, then all the works on neural network robustness verification with linear optimization, mixed integer linear programming and (symbolic) interval arithmetic should not be considered novel, as the basic theories were all proposed decades ago.

*Q: 1. The method seems not suitable for deep (reinforcement) learning practice...*

A: As we explained in the Introduction section, the paper aims at computing the reachable set overapproximations for NNCS instead of verifying deep neural networks. Regarding the neural network controller focused in this paper, the common scale of the problem in terms of the state space dimension studied in the control community is around 2-4. Please notice that verifying dynamical systems with even small-scale neural network controllers has already been a difficult task due to the complicated behavior generated by the interaction between the continuous dynamics and the neural network.

We do not agree with the claim by the reviewer that our approach is not scalable due to the recursive computation of the Taylor model coefficients. Firstly, the Taylor model coefficients are not computed recursively, there are several efficient methods presented in the existing work such as Makino \& Berz (2003); Chen (2015). Secondly, the complexity of Taylor model arithmetic in neural network is polynomial with the state dimension and polynomial order, and linear with the number of neurons, where any higher order monomial will be truncated in each multiplication under a given order bound. We are unclear how the conclusion "the computation order is quadratic w.r.t. the Taylor polynomial degree" is observed, we would be very grateful if the reviewer can provide us a detailed analysis.

Finally, we believe the complexity of POLAR is reasonable for the benefit of obtaining a precise function (over)approximation of the neural-network controller in NNCS reachability analysis. We validate this claim by demonstrating in the experimental results that POLAR outperforms the prior SOTA methods including ReachNN* and Verisig 2.0 by several orders of magnitude, as shown in Table 1 of the submission.

content.title: thanks for clarifications
content.comment:
Thanks for clarifying the differences between the current and the ReachNN* paper. I see that there is an improvement in how Bernstein's polynomials are applied here, compared to ReachNN*. The interval bounds are not just 'pushed through' the nonlinear controller network Bernstein approximation (ReachNN*), but the computed Bernstein approximation is integrated with the Taylor model of the plant (POLAR). This slightly improves my novelty assessment; the remaining claimed novelties of the paper I see as incremental. This also convinces me that the paper requires a significant rewrite to clarify how POLAR works 'under the hood' and why it is relevant for deep RL. I mean in particular:
* the paper lacks mathematical formalism, with not enough precise statements as definitions/lemmas/theorems with step-by-step proofs  and heavily rely on the assumption of reader's knowledge of the related work, '
* the benchmarks presentation, the dynamical systems, initial conditions, how were NNCSs trained are not presented, there are no  reach-tube tightness metric and numbers provided,  no discussion why the studied benchmarks are significant for deep RL practice (this still confuses me a lot). 

I see that verifying dynamical systems with even small-scale neural network controllers is already hard and appreciated in the control community. However, I like to see a discussion how is the NNCSs applied to small dynamical systems studied herein related to problems encountered in ML/RL, or at least a discussion of what needs to be done before applying this in practice.

_Finally, we believe the complexity of POLAR is reasonable for the benefit of obtaining a precise function (over)approximation of the neural-network controller in NNCS reachability analysis_
I am still not convinced this claim applies in the domain of robotic RL simulators. The typical state-space dimension of the plant encountered there is much larger than the studied 3/4 dims. 

Regarding the quadratic Taylor order I mean, that a recursive computation of the $p$-th order Taylor model approximation will require a $\mathcal{O}(p^2)$ plant-NNCS vector field evaluations, i.e., computing the p-th order coefficient of a nonlinear function expansion requires an order of $p$ computations. All of the smaller orders precomputed, i.e., $\sum_{i=1}^p{i}=\mathcal{O}(p^2)$.  In this regard, more commonly employed in deep learning, Eurler/Runge-Kutta schemes may be more plausible here, as they do not require computation of higher-order coefficients.

content.title: To Reviewer zrk4. (part 1)
To Reviewer zrk4. (part 2)
content.comment:
*Q: Regarding the quadratic Taylor order I mean, that a recursive computation of the -th order Taylor model approximation will require a plant-NNCS vector field evaluations, i.e., computing the $p$-th order coefficient of a $\mathcal{O}(p)$ nonlinear function expansion requires an order of $p$ computations. All of the smaller orders precomputed, i.e., $\sum_{i=1}^pi=\mathcal{O}(p^2)$
. In this regard, more commonly employed in deep learning, Eurler/Runge-Kutta schemes may be more plausible here, as they do not require computation of higher-order coefficients.*

A: The Taylor Models (TMs) produced by POLAR is **NOT** computed in such a way. As it is described in the paper, the TMs under continuous dynamics are computed by the TM flowpipe construction technique that was firstly proposed  Berz & Makino (1998) and then improved later in Chen(2015); Chen & Sankaranarayanan (2016). The TM coefficients are evaluated by a method called automatic differentiation, and the remainder is evaluated by verifying the contractiveness of Picard operation. Since all of these methods already exist, we only provided its high-level framework in the Preliminaries section. Notice that, it is not necessary to compute the coefficients for all of the monomials in a Taylor expansion, and the monomials which have 0 coefficients in a lower-order derivatives can be ignored. This is also the reason why Taylor approximations often have a much better performance than the other polynomial approximation forms for multivariate functions. Moreover, the complexity you pointed out is not related to the neural network depth. As mentioned in our previous reply, the use of TM arithmetic is associated with a max order, and the complexity of TMs does not grow along with the layer-by-layer propagation due to the order bound. In addition, Euler, Runge-Kutta, or other numerical integration methods can only generate state approximations, but our purpose is to compute reachable set overapproximations, which is much more challenging.

Finally, we would like to emphasize that POLAR is proposed for **verifying** NNCS, **NOT synthesizing** NNCS. Training a suitable neural network controller for a given continuous dynamics is not the goal of this paper.

content.title: To Reviewer zrk4 (Part 2)
content.comment:
*Q: There are no details given of how one of the crucial parts of the algorithm - the linear-nonlinear part decomposition is being performed. This computation may be of significant complexity.*

A: Any polynomial $p$ with bounded degree can be simply and uniquely decomposed to two polynomials $p_L$ and $p_o$ such that $p_L$ consists of only the linear terms in $p$ and $p_o$ keeps the other terms (constant and nonlinear terms). Therefore, this decomposition has a complexity which is linear in the number of terms in $p$. We already explained it in the first and second paragraphs in Section 3.2.

*Q: 2. Novelty.*

A: As we mentioned in the beginning, the review misunderstands both this paper and ReachNN*. We refer the clarification in the beginning as the response to the novelty concern.



*Q: 3. Related work is not presented*

A: We do not claim that using TM for the nonlinear dynamical system part in an NNCS is a contribution of this work. We also describe how this works in the **Preliminaries** section (not the section that describes our approach) and note that TM-based flowpipe construction has been used for ODEs in the last paragraph of the same section.



*Q: 4. Not Clear Benchmarks*

A: We consider these benchmarks because they allow us to perform a fair comparison with prior works as these benchmarks are the same benchmarks used in the ReachNN paper Huang et al (2019b) and in the Verisig 2.0 paper Ivanov et al. (2021a). 


*Q: 5.   Choice of the employed benchmark metrics.*

A: Both efficiency and performance (e.g., the final enclosure volume mentioned by the reviewer) matter. That is why we give both the verification time cost and the reachable set plots (in Sec. C of the appendix). 



*Q: p.12/13 B.2 proof: No reference given for the ‘Base Case’ part of the proof, i.e. that TM flow-pipe construction for the ode with control variable is sound. Another gap is an argument that the Bernstein polynomial interpolation layer-by-layer of the NN controller is also sound, this does not look obvious to me.*

A: The control variables are treated as additional state variables which are constant, i.e., have zero derivatives, in a control step. We will add more detailed explanations. The soundness proof of Univariate Bernstein polynomial for activation function approximation is given in the appendix (see Sec. B.1 of the appendix).

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a method for overapproximating outputs from small neural networks in the context of flowpipe construction of ODE systems controlled by neural networks.
content.main_review:
The paper proposed a method for overapproximating outputs from small neural networks in the context of flowpipe construction of ODE systems controlled by neural networks. The work is technically sound, but fairly misleading in the contributions, comparison with existing work, and important baselines are missing.

First of all, the context is for rigorously bounding reachable sets of ODE systems, which is an important and hard problem. However, the current work is only dealing with the problem of bounding the output of the control function, which is a simple feedforward neural network. In fact, one needs to read into the technical details to see that this is really what the paper is about, and the flowpipe construction part only serves as a context. This by itself is not a problem, but it does open up a huge range of recent literature on bounding outputs of neural networks in both the ML community and the formal methods community, and none of these have been mentioned. Of course, the authors emphasize that the current overapproximations are in function forms which is the key contribution, but I do not think that is difficult at all given the simplicity of Taylor models. 

Berstein polynomials themselves are very well-known as function approximators for global optimization (because the representation itself can be exponentially long). In fact, the ReachNN work https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.10654.pdf has already used Berstein polynomials for the same problem, and the main improvement in the current work is to use sets of univariate Berstein polynomials for coordinate-wise overapproximations to avoid the exponentially sized representation, but apparently at the cost of overapproximation by simple projections. It is really concerning that the authors highlight the comparison with Verisig in Figure 5, but avoid giving detailed conceptual explanation of the comparison with much more closely related approach of ReachNN and Sherlock. These tools only appear in the experiment section, and it of course does not help when we realize these are by almost the same set of authors (everything is on arxiv). 

Overall, apart from the questionable presentation that downplays similarity with the authors' previous work, the value of the paper can not be fairly evaluated before a lot more comparisons with SOTA tools on robustness analysis of neural networks are performed.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3942 by Reviewer Gf2A

content.title: To Reviewer Gf2A (Part 1)
content.comment:
*Q: First of all, the context is for rigorously bounding reachable sets of ODE systems, which is an important and hard problem. However, the current work is only dealing with the problem of bounding the output of the control function, which is a simple feedforward neural network. In fact, one needs to read into the technical details to see that this is really what the paper is about, and the flowpipe construction part only serves as a context.*

A: The close loop of a NNCS consists of a NN controller and a continuous system of which the dynamics is represented by an ODE. Thus, the reachable set computation of a NNCS involves the treatments of both NN controller and ODE. The flowpipe construction of an ODE has been studied in the past and we do not claim that as a contribution in this work. Therefore, we introduced it in the preliminary, rather than in the main technical section. 
We also want to emphasize that our work does not aim that bounding the output of the control function as the reviewer suggests, otherwise we can simply apply existing NN verification techniques to the NNCS reachability problem. In the second paragraph of the Introduction, we explain that directly using NN verification techniques is not effective for the NNCS problem due to their inability to carry dependencies across the closed-loop system and across multiple time steps. 
Another way to understand this is that bounding the output of the neural network does not tell us how the neural network function really behaves inside those bounds, so state-dependency is not well tracked by such a method.
Our contribution is a principled way of using polynomial overapproximation and propagation to overcome this issue. 

*Q: This by itself is not a problem, but it does open up a huge range of recent literature on bounding outputs of neural networks in both the ML community and the formal methods community, and none of these have been mentioned. Of course, the authors emphasize that the current overapproximations are in function forms which is the key contribution, but I do not think that is difficult at all given the simplicity of Taylor models.*

A: The application of NN output range analysis to NNCS reachability has been studied in the NNCS community. 
Similar to our response above, we explain why a direct application of these methods is not effective for solving the NNCS reachability problem because of their inability to carry dependency across the closed-loop system and across multiple time steps. 
Since an output range does not keep track of the dependency in the input-output mapping of a neural network, 
it would result in rapid error accumulations when used to compute the reachable sets of a dynamical system over multiple time steps.
Empirically, directly applied NN output range analysis to NNCS reachability 
has resulted in poor performance as demonstrated by existing literature such as Sherlock (Dutta et al. 2019a) (Sec. 1.2, Fig 2) and ReachNN (Huang et al. 2019b) (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 3).
NNV (Tran et al. 2020), which we compare with and discuss in the Experiments section, essentially uses this approach and fails to verify any of the benchmarks in Table 1 and the similar results can be found in Ivanov et al. 2021a (see the bottom paragraph on page 8).

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3942 by Reviewer Gf2A

content.title: To Reviewer Gf2A (Part 2)
content.comment:
*Q: Berstein polynomials themselves are very well-known as function approximators for global optimization (because the representation itself can be exponentially long). In fact, the ReachNN work https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.10654.pdf has already used Berstein polynomials for the same problem, and the main improvement in the current work is to use sets of univariate Berstein polynomials for coordinate-wise overapproximations to avoid the exponentially sized representation, but apparently at the cost of overapproximation by simple projections..*

A: First, our work is NOT an extension of the ReachNN work. The approaches in ReachNN and in POLAR are fundamentally different. As mentioned in Sec. 1, Para.3, ReachNN belongs to direct end-to-end approximation, while POLAR belongs to layer-by-layer propagation.
At a high level, ReachNN tries to approximate the input-output mapping of a neural network as a Bernstein polynomial directly through sampling in the input space, whereas POLAR is primarily based on propagating Taylor models.
In POLAR, univariate Bernstein polynomials are only used, as one of the many steps in the proposed framework, to deal with non-differentiable activation functions.  To further highlight the difference in terms of their resulting efficiency, the complexity of ReachNN's approach,
both in terms of the sampling-based error analysis and the size of Bernstein polynomials, grows exponentially with the input dimension, whereas the computation of univariate Bernstein polynomials in POLAR completely sidesteps this complexity issue because the input dimension of an activation function is one (discussed in Sec. 3.1).
The fact that univariate Bernstein polynomial is a special case of multivariate Bernstein polynomial only matters in terms of proving the soundness of the error estimation when Bernstein polynomials are used, and does not mean that the approach in ReachNN is similar to the approach in POLAR.
The fundamental difference between the usage of Bernstein polynomials in POLAR and in ReachNN is also one of the reasons that POLAR outperforms ReachNN by several orders of magnitude, as shown in Table 1 of the submission.



*Q: It is really concerning that the authors highlight the comparison with Verisig in Figure 5, but avoid giving detailed conceptual explanation of the comparison with much more closely related approach of ReachNN and Sherlock. These tools only appear in the experiment section, and it of course does not help when we realize these are by almost the same set of authors (everything is on arxiv)*

A: We do compare POLAR with ReachNN carefully in both the main **technical section** (Sec. 3.1) and the **Experiments section**.
ReachNN, cited as Huang et al. (2019a),
is a regular conference paper that describes the Bernstein polynomial approximation-based technique in detail. 
ReachNN*, cited as Fan et al. (2020a), is a tool paper that describes GPU acceleration and other optimizations on top of the prototype described in the ReachNN paper. 
Thus, we are **doing the best possible comparison** that we can, which is to compare with ReachNN when discussing the technical details, and compare with ReachNN* (the optimized tool) in the experiments.

content.title: To Reviewer Gf2A (Part 3a)
content.comment:
*Q: Overall, apart from the questionable presentation that downplays similarity with the authors’ previous work, the value of the paper can not be fairly evaluated before a lot more comparisons with SOTA tools on robustness analysis of neural networks are performed.*

A: 
We completely disagree with the statement that we are downplaying similarity with our previous work (see our response to the previous question). The reviewer is also making an assumption that SOTA tools on robustness analysis of neural networks will automatically translate to good performance on NNCS reachability analysis. This assumption has been shown to be wrong by existing literature and we also compare with an approach (NNV) that implements essentially that in our Experiments section.
In terms of novelty, 
as emphasized in the Introduction, ReachNN and POLAR are two completely different techniques. ReachNN uses direct end-to-end approximation (by sampling the input space), whereas POLAR uses layer-by-layer propagation of Taylor models. 
These are in fact the two main categories of approaches in NNCS verification literature. 
To further highlight the difference in terms of their resulting efficiency, the complexity of ReachNN's approach,
both in terms of the sampling-based error analysis and the size of Bernstein polynomials, grows exponentially with the input dimension, whereas the computation of univariate Bernstein polynomials in POLAR completely sidesteps this complexity issue because the input dimension of an activation function is one.
The fact that univariate Bernstein polynomial is a special case of multivariate Bernstein polynomial only matters in terms of proving the soundness of the error estimation when Bernstein polynomials are used, and does not mean that the approach in ReachNN is similar to the approach in POLAR.
The fundamental difference between the usage of Bernstein polynomials in POLAR and in ReachNN is also one of the reasons that POLAR outperforms ReachNN by several orders of magnitude, as shown in Table 1 of the submission.

content.title: To Reviewer Gf2A (Part 3b, for the same question in Part 3a)
content.comment:
We want to emphasize that 
NN robustness verification and NNCS verification 
are two very different problems.
The fundamental difference lies in whether the problem considers the interaction of the neural network with a (possibly nonlinear) continuous dynamical system
over multiple time steps.
Keeping track of state dependencies across the closed-loop system over multiple steps is vital for obtaining tight overapproximations of the reachable sets. 
While it is tempting to think of NNCS verification as an application of 
existing NN verification techniques, 
the difference between the two problems can result in markedly different approaches on how to (over-)approximate the neural network.
In particular, one can consider three types of output ranges for a neural network $f$ and an input region $X$: (1) a concrete range $Y$ such that $\forall x\in X, f(x) \in Y$, (2) a symbolic range $Y$ such that the bounds of $Y$ are represented symbolically based on $x$, e.g., for the linear/quadratic relaxation or symbolic interval analysis works mentioned by the reviewer, $\forall x \in X$, $g_1(x) \leq f(x) \leq g_2(x)$, where $g_1(x)$ and $g_2(x)$ are different linear/quadratic functions of $x$, and (3) $\forall x \in X$, $f(x) \in p(x) + I$, where $p(x)$ is a polynomial approximation of $f(x)$ and $I$ is an interval that encapsulates the approximation error (note that the symbolic remainder method in our paper is different from the symbolic interval in (2)).
Existing works on NN verification fall under either (1) or (2), where (2) can produce tighter bounds than (1) when the symbolic bounds are concretized. 
However, only (1) and (3) can be integrated directly with existing reachability analysis for nonlinear continuous systems such as Flow* (Chen et al. 2013) or CORA (Althoff et al. 2018) to perform reachability analysis of the overall NNCS. 
There is no existing technique that can handle the set representation in (2) for reachability analysis of nonlinear continuous systems, unless the bounds are concretized in which case it would suffer the same problem as (1).
In addition, existing symbolic output range analysis techniques such as CROWN assume that the input region $X$ is a concrete ball or box.  However, the reachable set of a nonlinear system in each step is represented in a symbolic form that helps keep track of state dependencies and this set can be highly non-convex. 
How to properly handle non-convex symbolic representations as input sets to a neural network has not been studied in existing output range analysis literature to the best of our knowledge.
Thus, integrating existing symbolic output range analysis techniques with reachability analysis for continuous nonlinear systems would face challenges on both ends of the interaction -- propagating the result of NN output range analysis to dynamical system reachability analysis, and propagating the result of dynamical system reachability analysis to NN output range analysis. Finally, it should be clear that the representation in (2) is different from the representation in (3), and (2) cannot be easily converted to (3), especially when $p(x)$ is a higher-order polynomial (see [this anonymous link](https://1drv.ms/b/s!AhlLtryzQXzwkkZEdHrvCHFvvGT9?e=yX8pyJ) for an illustration of the one-dimensional case).  While (2) may perform better than (3) in terms of estimating output ranges, (3) is critical to NNCS verification, thanks to its ability of propagating state dependencies in a closed loop control system.

Again, what we want to emphasize is that NN robustness verification and NNCS verification are different problems. Our approach is designed specifically for NNCS verification. 
On the other hand, applying current NN robustness verification techniques to NNCS verification faces a number of challenges as described above, and requires further studies that are beyond the scope of this paper. We will add a summary of this discussion in the revision to clarify the difference between of the two problems and further explain the motivation for our approach. 

M. Althoff, D. Grebenyuk and N. Kochdumper. Implementation of Taylor Models in CORA 2018. In Proc. of the 5th International Workshop on Applied Verification for Continuous and Hybrid Systems, pages 145–173, 2018.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes POLAR, a reachability analysis framework for neural network-controlled systems. POLAR improves the previous Taylor model overapproximation approach in two aspects: 1) use Bernstein polynomial to overapproximates activation function; 2) use symbolic remainders to mitigate the so-called wrapping effect, that is, instead of computing an overapproximated interval at each step, keep track of linear transformation matrices to delay overapproximation as late as possible. The experimental evaluation compares POLAR with three other recent work and shows that POLAR achieves the best performance on almost all tasks.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper makes relatively incremental contributions to the verification of neural network-controlled systems. Introducing Bernstein polynomials and the symbolic remainder seems quite effective on the chosen benchmark. However, I am not quite familiar with the chosen benchmark and find it difficult to assess the significance of experimental evaluation.

content.title: To Reviewer MWuh
content.comment:
*Q: the chosen benchmark only consists of 6 problem instances, and the number of state variables of each problem is fairly small (i.e., 2 to 4).*

A: These are the full benchmarks used in the related work Huang et al. (2019b), Ivanov et al. (2019b). The dimensions of state variables in these benchmarks are common in a control system.

*Q: the argument that Taylor approximation requires the approximated function to be differentiable and thus is not applicable to ReLU function is not correct, because ReLU is differentiable almost everywhere (except for at zero).*

A: As the reviewer said, ReLU is not differentiable at zero, so ReLU is not differentiable rigorously speaking.
This is also why Verisig 2.0 cannot handle ReLU networks.

*Q: the name of "symbolic remainders" is a bit misleading or confusing, since there is really no symbolic value introduced, instead, just accumulates linear transformations to delay overapproximation.*

A: It is the terminology that is widely used in related works. The "symbolic remainder" here denotes that we use the matrix multiplication to represent the remainder until the final interval evaluation, rather than concretizing it during the propagation. 

*Q: an ablation study (e.g., disable Bernstein polynomials or symbolic remainder) would be helpful to better understand the performance improvement.*

A: We have done exactly that through the running example in Sec. 3: Example 1 is the running example with basic TM arithmetic, Example 2 is the running example with Bernstein polynomial added, and Example 3 is the running example with symbolic remainder additionally enabled.

display_title: SOTA techniques for NN verification do NOT translate to good performances on the NNCS problems

content.title: SOTA techniques for NN verification do NOT translate to good performances on the NNCS problems
content.comment:
We hope the following additional result will help dispel the misconception on applying NN verification techniques to NNCS reachability analysis. Basically, SOTA techniques for NN verification do **NOT** translate to good performances on the NNCS problems. This is primarily due to the fact that NN verification techniques only perform bound estimation, and **cannot track state-wise dependencies across the closed-loop system and across multiple time steps**, as we explain in the introduction of the paper and has been discussed in existing NNCS verification literatures. 

We ran Alpha-beta-CROWN (which just won the neural network verification competition at VNN-COMP earlier this year) with Flow* (with the same setting we used for the other tools including POLAR in the paper) on the same 6-dimensional attitude control example in the Experiments section of the paper. The range of $\omega_1$ (the left plot in Figure 5) for the resulting reachable set is given below. 

After 1 control step: [-0.452831, -0.193562]

After 2 control steps: [-0.457384, 0.055315]

After 3 control steps: [-0.463739, 0.30797]

Observe that the reachable set already exploded after a single control step due to precisely the lack of state-wise dependency tracking across the closed-loop system. After 3 control steps, the resulting reachable set grew beyond the bounds of the left plot in Figure 5, because such an approach also cannot track state-wise dependency across multiple time steps. In comparison, the reachable sets produced by POLAR wrap around the simulated trajectories tightly even after 30 control steps. 

This is why the prior best approaches in NNCS verification all use polynomial overapproximation of the NN controller in some way, either by direct end-to-end approximation or layer-by-layer propagation, as we describe in the introduction of the paper. In fact, the research focus has been on how to tighten the overapproximation error so that polynomial overapproximation does not **degrade to range or bound analysis**. We directly compare with all of these prior best approaches in our experiments and show that POLAR achieves **orders of magnitude improvement** both in terms of efficiency and tightness of the reachable sets produced.
